explanations.answer: Crown the best son and fight for Ahab's house
explanations.explanation: That's the letter, baker. Jehu tells them to "select the best and most worthy son of your master, set him on his father's throne, and fight for your master's house." (2 Kings 10:3) I think that reads like a dare wrapped in a polite envelope. Nobody mails a letter like that unless they're feeling mighty sure of themselves.

explanations.answer: Send the seventy sons away to Judah
explanations.explanation: Judah never comes up in this letter. Jehu wants a son picked, a throne filled and a fight started, and nobody gets packed off anywhere. The sons stay right in Samaria, where the officials can see them. If you were hunting for a travel plan, this letter doesn't have one.

explanations.answer: Hand their chariots and horses to Jehu
explanations.explanation: Jehu does mention the chariots and horses, but only as things the officials have. He's not asking for them. He tells them to use what they've got: pick the best son, put him on his father's throne and fight for Ahab's house. It's a lot like telling someone, "You've got a full oven, so go bake," and then waiting to see if they will.

The text says the opposite, friend. The officials "were terrified" (2 Kings 10:4), and then they send Jehu a message: "We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say. We will not make anyone king." (2 Kings 10:5) They had the walls and the weapons, but they didn't pick up either one.

Right, they don't get ready to fight at all. The text says they were terrified, and then they send Jehu a message: "We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say." (2 Kings 10:5) They even add, "We will not make anyone king." A city full of chariots, and the whole plan was to say yes.

Two is the number they say. The text says they "reasoned, 'If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?'" (2 Kings 10:4) I think they mean Joram and Ahaziah, the two kings Jehu's side had just shot down (2 Kings 9:24, 27). Their math was short and it was scary.

Close, but they only count two. Their words are, "If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?" (2 Kings 10:4) I think they're counting the two kings who had already fallen to Jehu's side (2 Kings 9:24, 27). They didn't need a third to get the point.

Seven's a nice number, but it isn't theirs. The officials say "two kings," not seven. (2 Kings 10:4) The number seventy does show up in this passage, but that's Ahab's sons. The officials' count is two, and it scared them plenty.

That's the promise. They tell Jehu, "We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say. We will not make anyone king." (2 Kings 10:5) Jehu's first letter had told them to crown the best son, and here they turn it down. They add, "Do whatever is good in your sight."

Leaving town never comes up. Their message to Jehu says they'll do whatever he says and won't make anyone king. Samaria is where they stay, and I think they were holding on to their city pretty tightly right then.

Judah isn't in this message at all. The officials write to Jehu, and what they promise is that they "will not make anyone king." (2 Kings 10:5) No letters to other kingdoms, no help called in. Their whole reply is addressed to Jehu.

Yes, they do. The text says that when the letter arrived, "they took the sons of the king and slaughtered all seventy of them." (2 Kings 10:7) I think this is one of the heavy parts of the Bible, and it's okay to feel that. It shows how far the officials' fear took them.

The text says they did it. When the letter arrived, "they took the sons of the king and slaughtered all seventy of them." (2 Kings 10:7) Then they put the heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu at Jezreel. This is a hard verse, friend, and I think it should feel hard.

explanations.answer: Conspired against his master and killed him
explanations.explanation: Those are his words. Jehu tells the people, "It was I who conspired against my master and killed him." (2 Kings 10:9) The master he means is Joram, the king of Israel (2 Kings 9:24). He owns that part out loud, and then he turns around and asks who killed the others.

explanations.answer: Sent his men to burn down Samaria
explanations.explanation: Nobody burns anything in this scene. Samaria is still standing, and Jehu's speech is about two things. First, he says he conspired against his master and killed him. Second, he asks who killed all the others. Fire isn't in it.

explanations.answer: Broke his promise to the elders
explanations.explanation: The text never has Jehu making a promise to the elders, so there's nothing for him to break. What he admits is this: "It was I who conspired against my master and killed him." (2 Kings 10:9) The elders did send him a message promising to do whatever he said, but that was their promise to him.

He does say it. Jehu tells the people, "Know, then, that not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail…" (2 Kings 10:10) Ahab was an earlier king of Israel (1 Kings 16:29). The part to catch is whose words Jehu says are standing: the LORD's.

The text says he does. Jehu tells the people, "Know, then, that not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail…" (2 Kings 10:10) He goes on to say that the LORD has done what He promised through His servant Elijah. So the LORD's word is exactly what Jehu points to.

That's him. Jehu says the LORD "has done what He promised through His servant Elijah." (2 Kings 10:10) Elijah was the prophet who stood up to Ahab (1 Kings 18:36). The passage ends by pointing back to him too, with "the word that the LORD had spoken to Elijah." (2 Kings 10:17)

Samuel was a prophet in Israel (1 Samuel 3:20), but he isn't the name Jehu says. Jehu says the LORD promised it "through His servant Elijah." (2 Kings 10:10) The verse sticks with Elijah, and the end of the passage does too. Samuel's story is somewhere else in the Book.

Isaiah was a prophet too, the son of Amoz (Isaiah 1:1), but Jehu doesn't name him. He says the LORD has done what He promised "through His servant Elijah." (2 Kings 10:10) That's the name to keep in your pocket for this passage.

explanations.answer: Relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. "We are relatives of Ahaziah," they answer. (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah whose men had shot him earlier in the story (2 Kings 9:27). I think they had no idea what kind of answer that was to give Jehu.

explanations.answer: Servants of Hazael king of Aram
explanations.explanation: Hazael was king of Aram, a neighboring kingdom, but nobody at Beth-eked claims to be his servant. The men tell Jehu, "We are relatives of Ahaziah." (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah. They're family from the south, and Aram's king isn't in this scene.

explanations.answer: Prophets from the city of Bethel
explanations.explanation: No prophets are in this scene. Jehu asks, "Who are you?" and they answer, "We are relatives of Ahaziah." (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah. Bethel sounds a little like Beth-eked, but the text sends them somewhere else.

Greet is the word. They say, "…we have come down to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother." (2 Kings 10:13) That sounds like a friendly visit, like stopping by a neighbor's house with a plate of cookies. I think they had no idea what they were walking into.

Fighting isn't what they say they came for. They say they came "to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother." (2 Kings 10:13) A visit like that doesn't sound like a battle plan. It sounds like a family stopping by to say hello.

They don't say anything about a warning. Their words are, "…we have come down to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother." (2 Kings 10:13) Greeting is a visit, and warning is a message. Their reason is a simple hello.

He does. Jehu asks, "Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?" and Jehonadab answers, "It is!" (2 Kings 10:15) Jehonadab was the son of Rechab. He came walking up to meet Jehu on his own, and he said it with an exclamation mark.

The text says he says yes. Jehu asks, "Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?" and Jehonadab replies, "It is!" (2 Kings 10:15) Then Jehu says, "give me your hand." There's no hesitating in that answer.
Not quite, friend. After Jehonadab gives his hand, "Jehu helped him into his chariot." (2 Kings 10:15) He doesn't send Jehonadab ahead anywhere. He says, "Come with me," and he has him ride along.

Right, nobody gets sent ahead. Jehonadab gives Jehu his hand, and Jehu helps him into his chariot. (2 Kings 10:15) Then Jehu says, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:16) Jehonadab gets a seat right next to the driver, and that's not a front-runner spot.

That's the invitation. Jehu says, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:16) It's said right as Jehonadab climbs aboard. Jehu is the one calling it zeal here, so those are his words about himself.

A throne isn't what Jehu offers to show. His words are, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:16) Samaria is where the chariot is headed, but the thing he invites Jehonadab to see is zeal. I think that's a bigger thing to announce than a chair.

Walls don't come up in the invitation. Jehu says, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:16) He's pointing at his zeal, not at any city's defenses. The chariot is also headed toward Samaria, not back to Jezreel.
